question.problem:
Find the general solution to the following equation. 

$$
x\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}-y\,,\,x>0
$$

*Hint: You may wish to make use of the substitution $z={y}^{3}.$*
question.worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{3}\,⟹\,y={z}^{1/3}\,.
$$

Differentiating $y(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3{z}^{2/3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Consequently, the original differential equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x(\frac{1}{3{z}^{2/3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}) & =\frac{1}{{z}^{2/3}}-{z}^{1/3} \\ \frac{x}{3{z}^{2/3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{z}^{2/3}}-{z}^{1/3}\end{aligned}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. First, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{3{z}^{2/3}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{z}^{2/3}}-{z}^{1/3} \\ \frac{x}{3}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1-z \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{x}\,z & =\frac{3}{x}\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
P(x)=\frac{3}{x},\,Q(x)=\frac{3}{x}\,.
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)dx} \\  & ={e}^{\int 3/xdx} \\  & ={e}^{3\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{3}} \\  & ={x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Under the condition that $x>0.$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x)={x}^{3}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{x}\,z) & ={x}^{3}\cdot \frac{3}{x} \\ {x}^{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+3{x}^{2}z & =3{x}^{2} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[{x}^{3}z] & =3{x}^{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[{x}^{3}z]\,\text{d}x & =\int 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\ {x}^{3}z & ={x}^{3}+C \\ z & =1+\frac{C}{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{3}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{3} & =1+\frac{C}{{x}^{3}} \\ y & =\sqrt[3]{1+\frac{C}{{x}^{3}}},\end{aligned}
$$
